justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish baseline across all three horizons, anchored around a current price in the low-to-mid 140s. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 142.5 essentially assumes mean reversion toward recent trading levels with minimal directional catalyst, implying very little expected movement from wherever the asset is currently trading. At the one-week horizon, I nudged the estimate slightly higher to 143.0, reflecting a weak upward drift assumption consistent with a modest positive trend or carry effect. At the one-month horizon, the estimate rises further to 144.5, incorporating a slightly larger expected drift while still treating the near-term environment as broadly stable. In each case, the point estimate is less a bold directional call and more a reflection of "current price plus modest drift," which is often the most defensible baseline in the absence of strong fundamental catalysts.

The confidence interval widths expand substantially as the horizon lengthens, which is standard given that uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the 90% interval spans only 8 points, reflecting that intraday and overnight volatility is relatively contained under normal market conditions. At one week, the interval widens to 16 points, incorporating the possibility of scheduled macro events, earnings, or policy announcements that could generate larger moves. At one month, the interval expands to 33 points, acknowledging that over four weeks, a wide variety of fundamental, technical, and sentiment shifts can accumulate and interact in nonlinear ways. The asymmetry in the intervals is relatively modest, suggesting I'm not pricing in a strong skew toward upside or downside at any horizon.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the downside, a sharper-than-expected deterioration in macro data — such as a surprise inflation print, an unexpected central bank policy shift toward greater tightening, or a geopolitical shock — could easily breach the lower bounds, particularly at the one-month horizon. Credit stress events or liquidity crunches in correlated assets could also produce fat-tail downside moves that my intervals don't fully capture. On the upside, a strong risk-on catalyst such as a dovish policy pivot, better-than-expected earnings, or a resolution of a geopolitical overhang could push prices well above the upper bounds. Tail events by definition fall outside 90% intervals roughly 10% of the time, so these scenarios are not implausible — they simply represent the excluded tails of the distribution I was implicitly modeling.
